I presented all the things of the gospel, I got all the key reports right. What's going on? He looked at me and said, seriously, Scott? What's going on? Because has there ever been a time in history when sinners like to be told they're sinners? And to the downtrodden church in Rome. And to the discouraged among us this morning, Mark reminds us that the way the gospel grows and the way the kingdom expands is a mystery. Jesus has taught this in the parables back in Mark 4. And now Mark illustrates it for us. That here the disciples go out and they're received. But Jesus comes to his own hometown and he's rejected. And from an earthy perspective, it makes no sense. And then Mark comes back around and wraps up the account with the story of John the Baptist. And how does he address John's situation? We know that he had disciples, and we know that he had followers, and we know that he had some success. But rather, Mark focuses in on the death of John at the hands of a corrupt and crooked king, Herodantopos. And the message to you and to me and to the original audience of the Gospel of Mark is a simple one. Again, do you think that you're going to present the Gospel better than John the Baptist? Do you think that your ability to transcend the difficulties of this life exceeds that of John the Baptist? Do you think that it comes down to you being rewarded for the excellent way that you tell your neighbors about the Lord? For if that's the argument, if you're supposed to have wonderful reception because you've done a great job of revealing the gospel, then John ought to be the most rewarded human in this life ever was. For no one has presented the Christ better except the Christ Himself. And how did John's lot end up in this life? Twelve pounds lighter than he should have been. For the loss of his head. And Mark writes to discouraged and downtrodden Christians, some of whom are sitting here this morning. And he says, do not judge your message on the way it's received. Do not judge the Holy Spirit on the things you perceive. It's not about how much our church grows or shrinks. We do not get to claim some mantle of righteousness because we have big numbers, nor are we to assume there's something wrong with us because we have small numbers, nor do we get to Reverse those things and say, well, our small numbers are the proof of our purity of our doctrine? No. The outcome is not necessarily related in human terms to the process We are called to proclaim the gospel, a gospel that calls people to repent of their sins and to know Jesus Christ. And there will be times in our lives and in our ministry, in our collectiveness as a church, where this will go forth and be well received, and the numbers will grow as they did for the apostles. But there will be times when we'll be rejected as Jesus was. And there will be times when that rejection will become so harsh as to go even to the point of death, as it did for John. So the question is not, how are things turning out? The question is not, are you having your best life now? The question is not, are you growing your ministry? Is your Sunday school class getting bigger? Is your women's Bible study growing? Are these things? The question is, are you proclaiming the truth of Jesus Christ? Are you calling people to repentance? And if they reject you for that reason, then it's a good day. And if they kill you for that reason, it is a good day. And if God blesses the growth of your ministry for that reason, then it's an equally blessed day. The success of the twelve is couched in the failure of Jesus himself in his hometown. And in the failure of John from an earthly perspective. And yet Jesus says what about John? There has never been one greater born of woman. And what does the Father say about Jesus? He ascends to the right hand of God, and from there he will come to judge the living and the dead. It is not how things appear in this life, but how God judges them to be. Let us be a church who proclaims the gospel of good news of repentance and of forgiveness without regard for how it is received or how it is rejected, but because that's the call upon the lives of those of us who confess Him to be Christ. Let's pray.

I don't like that song. Did you bother to wonder if God might like that song? Does it declare his praises? Does it speak highly of him? Does it exalt him? If you came to get, you're probably coming to a genie in a bottle. If you came to give, you probably have a better understanding of what we're really supposed to be doing here. We give him praise. Not half-hearted praise. Not pinched lip praise. Not praise full of excuses, well my voice isn't that great. Let me ask you this. And if you, as the flawed, sinful parents that you and I are, can love your child and be excited about the off-key performance of the school production How much more so our Heavenly Father, who is phenomenally gracious? Because if you restrain your voice in singing his praises because you're worried about what people think of you, You didn't come to give to God. And when you come here, do you give him your attention in the service? Are you sitting there going, what am I going to get out of this? It's going to make me feel good about myself. My wish today is that I feel better about myself. Pastor, say something to make me feel better about myself so I can walk through here and get my wish granted Stephen says, no, you guys have got this bottled-up view of God that he's contained in this temple. Yes, he has agreed. He graciously agreed to come meet with you in the temple. He has said that he would come down and be present there, but that's not because he's trapped inside. It's because he is the God of all the universe. And we would sit there going, so where do I actually focus my attention? I don't know where to go to know that I've actually and for our sake, he said, let me make it simple. Come to this spot. And I will meet with you there. Not for one moment because he's confined to it, because he has genie-like bracelets that keep pulling him back to the temple and he can't escape it. That's God in a bottle thinking. And we have to be careful that we don't fall into that. There's a great deal in the American church today that gets awfully close to that view of things. We must not. Do you notice all the warnings in the passage that the bottle was empty? Over and over and over again, Stephen tells them, You're not getting it. You're missing the point. Your bottle, you're hanging on to this bottle so you can control your genie God, but you've missed the fact that the bottle is empty. When God sends a man and says, Go this way, do these things, and you reject him You're hanging on to an empty bottle. When God sends Joseph and you reject him. When God sends Moses and you reject him. Oh, by the way, and when God sent Jesus and you rejected him. Many of us hang on to an empty bottle. Because we don't come to God through the mediator of his appointing. We don't come to God as the God of glory. We don't come with reverence and fear and adoration. When a plan to exalt, we come to get. We come as though He is answerable to us. Stephen says, when you come to God on your own terms, when you do not recognize that He has sent Jesus of Nazareth, when you do not recognize that that's the only way to come That the sacrifices of the temple, the sacrifices of your offering or my offering, the sacrifices of our time, the sacrifices of anything else we do are are nothing They gain us nothing with God. They're good in the sense that they're given in faith a response. But if we for one moment believe that they're what's going to get us into God's presence. We are horribly mistaken. We have an empty bottle, just as these people had. God in a bottle of thinking keeps God bound up in church. Leaves him there all week. He doesn't get to be a part of my life. I'm going to come in, meet with him for a short time on Sunday morning, and I'm going to walk out and leave him there. God in a bottle of thinking says he's just there to do what I want when I want it. And that's an empty bottle. That's one that Stephen says, no, no, no, that's getting you nowhere. And you notice what happened at the beginning of chapter 8. You notice how the passage that we read ends. And there arose on that day a great persecution against the church in Jerusalem. And they were all scattered throughout the regions of Judea and Samaria except the apostles. Many of us read that and go, how sad for the church. But that's not Luke's point. If you say how sad for the church, you've not read the rest of Acts. If you stop here, I can see how you get that conclusion. But we've got to remember this. This is the last time Jerusalem will be the point of attention in the book of Acts. This is the last time we will see ministry occurring in Jerusalem. The last time we will see people coming to the Lord. in Jerusalem. Oh, they're going to return to Jerusalem for trials. They're going to return to Jerusalem for controversy. They're going to return to Jerusalem for But never again were we going to see in the book of Acts that the Word of God is going forward in Jerusalem as it's going forward everywhere else. You see, they're not going to get the wish they're going to wish they had. Because when you reject God's man, When you reject him in the form of Jesus, when you reject him in the form of Peter, when you reject him in the form of John, and now when you reject him in the form of Stephen, at some point God stops sending people. At some point, he turns you over, just as we saw Stephen quoted in the Old Testament, God turned them over to the gods of Moloch and Russia, and I can't remember all the names of the other gods there. He's going to turn us over. If we reject Jesus of Nazareth, if we reject the teaching of this book, not only are we going to run out of the wishes for the things that make us happy in this life But we're going to find ourselves one day standing, really wishing we had a fourth wish. I wish I could go back and change my attitude. I wish I could go back and repent of my sin and humble myself before Jesus and go and cling to him in faith. I wish I could do that. And it'll be too late. The gospel will have moved on, just as it moves on from Jerusalem at this point. When we reject God's appointed Savior When we reject the one he sent and said, Come to him, come to me through him, not through your temple, not through the church of your making, not through the good deeds of your choosing Come through Jesus. When we reject that, we end up wishing we had more wishes. And it'll be too late. We must stop treating God as though He is our wish granter. Our genie. We must come to him through Jesus. Come to him because he is Almighty God. Come to him because he is worthy of anything that we would proclaim positively about him and worthy of so much more. We must do so with enthusiasm and excitement and knowledge and energy. Do so in here, do so out there, do so in here. So that we know he is not our genie. He is our God. He does not answer to us. We answer to him. Let's pray. Lord, forgive the way that we bottle you up. Think of you in small, confined ways. Think of you only being able to do what we ask you to do as though you could not possibly work unless we prayed first. Forgive us for that. Cut us free from that thinking. Let us see a God who is more capable. And more willing than we could ever imagine. It will be scary for a time, because we will feel like we're out of control. But God help us to recognize that the only way to a sure outcome is for you to be in control. Make us that kind of people, make us that kind of church. Let us hear the warning that Stephen gave to the Jewish Council. Let it be a warning to us. We pray this in Christ's name. Amen.

sermons.title: To Samaria...And Beyond!
sermons.speaker: Tom Poehlman
sermons.text: We remember as we consider God's Word that God's word not only is inerrant and holy and infallible, but it is the only. uh rule, the only infallible rule for um for faith and practice. If we want to know who God is, if we want to know what God is like, if we want to know um uh what he says about us And what he directs us to do, we need to know God's Word. Acts 8, beginning at verse 4. Now those who were scattered went about preaching the Word. Philip went down to the city of Samaria and proclaimed to them the Christ, and the crowds with one accord paid attention to what was being said by Philip when they heard him and saw the signs that he did. For unclean spirits, crying out with a loud voice, came out of many who had them, and many who were paralyzed or lame were healed. So there was much joy in that city. But there was a man named Simon, who had previously practiced magic in the city and amazed the people of Samaria, saying that he himself was somebody great. They all paid attention to him, from the least to the greatest, saying, This man is the power of God that is called great. And they paid attention to him because for a long time he had amazed them with his magic But when they believed Philip, as he preached good news about the kingdom of God and the name of Jesus Christ, they were baptized, both men and women. Even Simon himself believed, and after being baptized, he continued with Philip. And seeing signs and great miracles performed, he was amazed. Now, when the apostles at Jerusalem heard that Samaria had received the Word of God, they sent to them Peter and John, who came down and prayed for them that they might receive the Holy Spirit. For he had not yet fallen on any of them, but they had only been baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus. Then they laid their hands on them, and they received the Holy Spirit Now when Simon saw that the Spirit was given, through the laying on of the apostles' hands, he offered them money, saying, Give me this power also, so that any one on whom I lay my hands may receive the Holy Spirit. But Peter said to him, May your silver perish with you, because you thought you could obtain the gift of God with money. You have neither part nor lot in this matter, for your heart is not right before God. Repent, therefore, of this wickedness of yours, and pray to the Lord, that if possible the intent of your heart may be forgiven you. For I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of iniquity. And Simon answered, Pray for me to the Lord, that nothing of what you have said may come upon me. Now when they had Testified and spoken the word of the Lord, they returned to Jerusalem, preaching the gospel to many villages of the Samaritans Now an angel of the Lord said to Philip, Rise and go toward the south, to the road that goes down from Jerusalem to Gaza This is a desert place. And he rose and went. And there was an Ethiopian, a eunuch, a court official of Candace, queen of the Ethiopians, who was in charge of all her treasure. He had come to Jerusalem to worship, and was returning, seated in his chariot, and he was reading the prophet Isaiah. And the Spirit said to Philip, Go over and join this chariot. So Philip ran to him and heard him reading Isaiah the prophet and asked, Do you understand what you were reading? And he said, How can I unless someone guides me? And he invited Philip to come up and sit with him. Now the passage of the scripture that he was reading was this like a sheep he was led to the slaughter. And like a lamb before a cheerer is silent, so he opens not his mouth. In his humiliation justice was denied him. Who can describe his generation? For his life is taken away from the earth And the eunuch said to Philip, About whom I ask you, does the prophet say this? About himself or about someone else? Then Philip opened his mouth, and beginning with this scripture, he told him the good news about Jesus And as they were going along the road they came to some water, and the eunuch said, See, here is water. What prevents me from being baptized? And he commanded the chariot to stop, and they both went down into the water, Philip and the eunuch, and he baptized him And when they came up out of the water, the Spirit of the Lord carried Philip away, and the eunuch saw him no more, and went on his way rejoicing. But Philip Found himself at Azotis. As he passed through, he preached the gospel to all the towns until he came to Caesarea. Pray that God would be pleased. And would be honored with the reading of His Word. Let's pray. Lord, take your word and apply it to our hearts. May the Holy Spirit be our teacher. That we would hear what you would have us to hear and remember what you would have us to remember and act upon what you would have us to act upon. We pray these things in Jesus' name. Amen. Well, thank Pastor Shaw and the elders for the opportunity again to preach. I said to Pastor Shaw last week after he had that very lengthy passage, some 72 verses between Acts 6, 7, and the beginning of 8. I said, okay, you did 58 minutes last week on 72 verses, and I have 36 verses this week, does that mean I have 29 minutes? And at that point somebody else said I'd love to hear a sermon from only five verses. We trust that the Lord will bless whatever happens. It seems that life is full of two kinds of times. Times of status quo. When circumstances and routine seem pretty much the same, and times of transition, when you're preparing for and then beginning a new stage of your life You decide to move maybe to another um uh area close to where you live or maybe even across the country or around the world. In school, there are transitions as you begin elementary school and middle school and high school and college or vocational training Transition as you begin a career and certainly transition later on if you change a career. I understand that more and more people change their career multiple times during the course of their working years You decide to get married and during the engagement period it's a transition, preparing not just for a wedding, but for um for married life You have an accident or a major illness, and instead of life as usual, you have a time of healing and convalescence I remember one transition um uh that occurred in my family as um I had two younger sisters two years apart and in my day, which will tell you how old this is, we didn't have middle school, we had junior high which began at grade seven and went through grade nine. Now my one sister Janet um was going into grade nine and the ninth graders in middle school are are the the cream of the crop And my other sister Carol was going into grade seven. She was the newbie, the bottom of the barrel. So when Janet um uh gave Carol advice about um beginning this transition in junior high, she said, if you see me in the halls Don't wave. The time of trying a new church. Deciding whether this is the place that um that you want to be a part of is a transition. And for the early church, the events Luke describes beginning with chapter six and seven are a major transition No sooner, it seems, does uh the church selects seven men as deacons than one of them is brought to trial um for his forthright preaching of the gospel. He is violently and shockingly executed, and life changes entirely for the Christian community in Jerusalem. This morning we will look at um the work of another of these deacons, a man named Philip And the major transition of taking the gospel and the church out from Jerusalem. Times of transition can be difficult They can be unexpected as far as what will happen, what will happen afterward, how long the transition will take. But the thing to remember is that the Lord is there to bring us through those times of transition. They may catch us by surprise. They may not be what we expect, but nothing catches him by surprise. He ordains and plans all the things that happen, so we can trust him for our transitions as well as our um our times of status quo. And during times of transition, our circumstances and even our abilities may change But God will use us to serve Him in whatever conditions we find ourselves. As Scripture teaches us, all Christian believers have gifts and abilities um uh abilities and gifts to use to serve the Lord. That's what ministry is. The word that's translated ministry is the same word that elsewhere is translated serve or um or deacon serving the Lord in the places that He puts us and with the gifts that He gives us. So in that sense as I talk about ministry in terms of the the headings of the um the sermon today, not talking about ordained ministry, um talking about um the ministry, the service for all of God's people. The events in um in Acts chapter eight give us not only a historical account of the things that happened as the persecution began and as Philip carried the gospel to these different places. They also give us important lessons about the ministries that God gives us. Ministry in life sometimes take unexpected directions. You may very well have known that in your own life, and you may very well be experiencing that right now. Ministry can sometimes be challenging when it's with undesirable objects and people. We don't always get to choose the people that God brings us to to minister to. Ministry is not always neat and predictable. Sometimes its results are uncertain. But sometimes ministry serving the Lord can give us unparalleled opportunities. First, I want to look with you at the unexpected direction of ministry. Things in Jerusalem had been going remarkably well for quite some time. The church had grown, people were coming to faith, there were over five thousand people there, they were meeting together regularly They had dealt with an internal issue with the uh the selection of these deacons. There was an uneasy truce with the religious leaders there in the Sanhedrin after they had followed the advice of Gamaliel And even some of the priests were coming to the faith. Things were going about as well as you could possibly imagine if you were there. Then Stephen is arrested and martyred, and everything changes. We didn't read the first four verses of chapter eight, but um the second half of verse one um tells us that the um uh the people were scattered. They were dispersed. They were called the diaspora, those who had been dispersed in letters that um that are written later in the New Testament. They were dispersed much as the Jewish people were dispersed after the exile into Babylon. Says that all were dispersed except the apostles. And maybe you wonder why not the apostles? Well it seems that most of the um the difficulty that pe uh that people were experiencing was at the hands of Hellenistic Jews. All of the apostles were Hebraic Jews. What's more, they knew that even though a lot of people were being spread out, there were a lot of people still there, and Jerusalem was still um uh the center of the Christian faith at that point. So they stayed to provide the leadership that was necessary and uh uh to go on from there. There was ongoing violent persecution. Before, only when healings had been done or preaching had been done was there persecution and beatings on the hand at the hands formerly of the um uh the leaders of the uh the Jewish community. But now a systematic effort to seek and destroy begins, led by a man named Saul, about whom we will hear more next week. What was going on? One of the early Christian leaders, a man named Irenaeus, a century or so later, said, The blood of the martyrs is the seed of the church, and it is a quote that many other Christian leaders have used since then. Persecution instead of stopping the church caused the gospel to spread and caused more people to come to faith. We don't see that as much here in this country because the persecution is not nearly as Obvious and open, but in other parts of the world we see that very thing. In um the uh the middle of the last century, hundreds of missionaries were expelled from China. The thought was that um uh that this would put an end to the church in China. There are hundreds times the number of Christians in China today that there were when those missionaries were expelled. The blood of the martyrs, the persecution on God's people, is the seed of the church. If it was Satan's plan to stop the Christian faith's growth by this, it seems that he overreached. Jesus had said that they would carry the gospel to Jerusalem, to Judea, to Samaria, and to the ends of the earth It was this persecution that began to take this from Jerusalem to the next step. Now some people have thought that this means that The Lord was there waiting for the um the apostles and the others to get the idea, you've got to go out from here. After a while, they're just not getting it, so we better turn up the heat and make them do what they don't want to do That would be an indication that God changes his mind and doesn't have a plan. Scripture doesn't say that. What we believe is that this persecution was the means that God used. It's not the means that um uh that they liked. It's not the means that um that uh that we would have um going if we were um uh if we were having a session meeting to plan how the church uh how our church would uh go on from here. We wouldn't say, well you know, we're just not growing fast enough. We need to bring in some people to make it hard for everybody We wouldn't do that. But that was the means that God chose. And because he is sovereign, and because he knew what would happen, he planned what would happen. He brought about what would happen. That persecution accomplished great and mighty things. Theologian John Stott sees a pattern here in Acts 8. Martyrdom leads to persecution Persecution leads to scattering, and scattering leads to widespread evangelism In the fall, I frequently see leaves all over our deck and all over the porch. And so when Julie says to me, get a blower out there and get those off of there, it would be nice if as soon as you turned the blower on, all the leaves went in the same direction. and left the deck or left the porch completely. Have you had the experience with a blower that I've had? You turn the blower on and they go every place. Well Satan and Saul and those who were with them turned on the heat, and the Christians and the gospel went every place. Part of transitions are the changes, either temporary or permanent, that they bring, often with uncertainty Where are we going? How long will he be there? What will I do next? What will I be able to do next? Circumstances may change, but God doesn't change. We need to trust him through the transitions. and when they even when they go in unexpected directions. Secondly, we see the undesirable objects of ministry. One commentator wrote that Jesus regarded uh or that Jews rather regarded Samaritans as heretical outsiders, and Ethiopia as the extreme southern boundary of the habitable world. And that's where Philip headed. Jews and Samaritans had a history and it wasn't a nice history. It got worse when David's grandson Rehoboam Listen to bad advice, and the kingdom divided into a southern kingdom of Judah with the tribe of Judah and the tribe of Benjamin, and the northern kingdom of Israel with all of the others It was the northern kingdom of Israel that eventually established the city of Samaria and from which they got the name Samaritans. It was the northern kingdom that was taken into exile first. by the um by the Assyrians. The NIV and some of the other translations say that what he practiced was sorcery. So this is not the illusion that you see magicians today practicing. This is something deeper. All use the same Greek word, exestami, which means amazed or astonished. In verse 9, Simon amazed the people there in that city. In verse 11, they were amazed by him. This incident with Simon is the second controversial thing in Acts chapter 8. The first controversy was, is it one step or two-step? to um believe and receive the Holy Spirit. The second controversy is was Simon a believer or not? Verse 13 says he believed. It says he was baptized. Stroll said years ago, we are saved not by a profession of faith, but by a possession of faith. Signs and miracles point to Jesus, but if you don't get past the signs, you never really get to Him. So We need to ask ourselves, do I love God more now than I used to? Do I love God's Word more now than I used to? Do I love God's people more now than I used to? Do I want to follow the Lord more faithfully now than I used to? Was Simon a true believer? Well, look at his reaction to Peter in verse 24. sermons.text: Turn in your Bibles this morning to Matthew 28. Matthew 28, the first book of the New Testament, the last chapter of that book. We'll be looking at verses 16 through 20. Matthew 28, 16 through 20. We have started this year with a little sermon series called 2020 Vision, seeing as God sees. We have been trying to take a look at a handful of different topics and to try to recalibrate how we think about them in a more biblical way, to try to look at what the Bible has to say about these things. And so we saw in the first week the need to see the Savior, to see Jesus as the only one who can redeem fallen humanity. In the second week we took a look at the need to see the bride, to see the church as this glorious one who will be united to Jesus for all of eternity. In our third week, last week, we took a look at the our need to see the image of God in our fellow man. and then to treat our fellow man as though they reflect the handiwork and art, artistry of our God. This morning we're going to look at our mission. Seeing the mission. What is the mission of the church? And to help us understand that, we're going to look now at Matthew 28, starting in verse 16. Now the eleven disciples went to Galilee, to the mountain to which Jesus had directed them. And when they saw him, they worshiped him, and some doubted. And Jesus came and said to them, all authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have commanded you. And behold, I am with you always to the end of the age. This is the word of God. Praise be to God. Let's pray and ask his guidance and understanding it. Lord, show us your word this morning. By your power, let it get past our stopped ears and penetrate our hard hearts That it would convict us of sin where we have sin. But once we are convicted, Lord, let it also show us. The great confidence we have in the one who has saved us and made us his own. We pray this in Jesus' name. Amen. So what is our main purpose as a church? What is the basic reason we exist? As a general rule, there are two answers given most often among churches today to that question. One of those answers goes like this. The main purpose of the church is to find the lost. The function of the church, the reason the church exists, is for evangelism. This view tends to skew everything in the church to being all about the unbeliever, the non-churchgoer. You who are sleeping in on Sunday morning and waiting only for football. What can we do to entice you? How can we bring you in? What do you want? Or perhaps we're going to sound a little bit uh more righteous about it, what do you need? As if fallen man knows his own needs And we appeal and say, we're going to make the church all about being appealing to the lost so that they will come in. And that inevitably leads to churches that look an awful lot like the world. In our attempt to accommodate them, we end up looking like them. Charles Spurgeon, more than a century ago, warned, one reason why the Church of God has so little influence over the world is because the world has so much influence over the church. The risk of the church being driven by evangelism is that we will sell out in order to attract the unbeliever. This error arises because we do not properly understand our mission. Evangelism by itself is not the main purpose of the church. Now let me say that again. Many of you have been in church a long time, and when you hear Matthew 28, 16 to 20 read, what you expect to hear next is that you must be all about evangelism. I didn't say we shouldn't be about evangelism. What I did say is that evangelism by itself is not the main purpose. of the church. It is not solely the content of our mission. Now the second answer that's often given to the question, what is it we should be about, is that the church is all about discipleship. The church exists to make believers stronger. The church exists to build up the body of Thus, in this scenario, the question is not, unbeliever, what do you need? But as believer, what do you think you need? What do you want? How can we serve you as a believer? And when you frame it up that way, you realize that it is also an error. For it is just the reflection of the first view. Each of them is a marketing ploy. They just have a different market niche. The first view says our market is the unbeliever, the second view says our market is the believer, but they're both driven by the wants or perceived needs of humanity. And both, therefore, are flawed. When we become discipleship focused, us focused We tend to abandon evangelism and we devolve into what J. D. Greer, he's the president of the Southern Baptist Convention, what J. D. Greer has called not a church, but just a group of disobedient Christians hanging out. Both views are consumer driven. Both views are about people. And therefore, both views fail. So, what is the purpose of the church? What is its mission? Well, we saw two weeks ago that the church is the bride. of Christ, a bride adorning herself, making herself beautiful for her bridegroom. The purpose of the church is to please Jesus. The purpose of the church is to satisfy and make him happy. He's, if you want to put it in the business model I spoke of a moment ago, he's the consumer. He's the target audience The purpose of the church is to please Jesus Now what pleases Jesus? What makes him happy? He tells us in the passage, he says to his disciples, Go therefore and make disciples of all nations, baptizing the name of the Father and of the Son and the Holy Spirit, teaching them to observe all that I have said. Commanded you. The question is not evangelism or discipleship, but it is evangelism and discipleship. For what purpose and in what context? Worship. What did we see here? It's that the expectations went out of line with his word. The expectations were not in a line with who he had revealed himself to be. And it is my fear, and it is my concern that many who call themselves Christians Are one day going to turn and jump to the other side and scream, Crucify Him! For he will not meet their expectations, and they will judge him to be a failure. Are you expecting Jesus to keep you from getting sick? Are you expecting Jesus to guard your wealth in this world and in this life? He never promised to do either of those things. And you will be disappointed. But if you are expecting Jesus to provide a next life, Where wealth will overflow and never be at risk, where health will be guaranteed for all of eternity. If that's what you're expecting out of Jesus, then you will not be disappointed. For that's what He has promised, and that's what He will deliver. We must remember the journey, an intense, important, and intriguing journey, which focuses us so that we listen. We must remember the teaching, and it was uh principally about the kingdom of God. We must remember the entry which was staged so that we would get a glimpse of his glory. We must remember the warnings that if we do not respond rightly, we'll be replaced by the stones, and we must remember the anger that comes when we don't align our expectations with his promises. But all of this will come by remembering the glory. All of this will come by remembering the glory. Focus on who Jesus is, not on what you want Him to do for you. Focus on what Jesus has actually done at the cross and not on what you want him to be. Know the Word of God so well that you know who Jesus is and what He has promised. His promise is forgiveness of sins for those who believe in him. His promise is eternal life for those who receive him. His promise is not health and wealth and well-being in this life. But his promises that those who will trade the things of this life will get many times more in the next And we remember the glory of Jesus when we see him for who he is and not what he can do for us. Then all the rest of this is going to fade away. All the rest of this is going to be hard to see because of the brilliance of the one we're looking at And it's going to be easy to expect him to be king of our life, of our world, of our eternity. Palm Sunday, the triumphal entry, it is a glimpse of glory. See the glory and respond rightly in true worship. Let's pray. Lord Jesus We do not see you as the glorious one you are. We do not treat you as one worthy of glorification. We do not offer to you enthusiastic praise, especially when we're not getting what we want. Lord, undo our expectations Change us to be people who understand who you are and what you've done and why you came, and in understanding those things rightly. We have certainty that you will meet those expectations. Let us get a glimpse of your glory on this Palm Sunday So that we will rightly understand who you are, rightly glorify you for who you are, rightly praise you for who you are. And we will never be disappointed when we do that. We pray this in your wonderful, glorious name. Amen.

sermons.text: We've taken a break uh from our study of Acts this Holy Week to look at Luke's account of the events of Holy Week and invite you to open your Bibles to Luke 24, Luke chapter 24 We'll be reading various verses from that in just a moment. Events that are happy, good events, events that we're excited about, things that we are glad to have happen to us, they need no warning. We don't have to be told that they're coming. When they happen, we rejoice in them. And yet, bad things that are going to happen to us, we receive them much more easily if we have some warning they're coming. There's a reason the doctor says those little words, you're going to feel a little something, embraces us to get ready for that pain. The one who uh we see the incoming for weeks or months in advance, it's sad, and yet we can prepare ourselves to deal with it. When good news, when good things happen, we don't need to be warned that they're going to happen. But when bad things are going to happen There is some comfort in knowing that it's coming. If you want to deter foolishness, impart wisdom. And where does wisdom begin? With the fear of the Lord. It is his hope that at least a few in his audience fear the Lord and will be deterred from the foolishness of apostasy. And that raises the question of the nature of the fear of the Lord. What is the fear of the Lord? It is most often described in churches and Christian writing as reverent awe. But I ask you, is Reverend Awe an effective deterrent? I am in awe of Niagara Falls. But does my awe keep me from jumping over the edge? Why haven't more people attempted to ride over the falls? Awe? I don't think so. Fear. That's what keeps us from doing foolish things. And that's what our author is conjuring up in his readers' minds. Fear. I know this view of the fear of the Lord is going to be a little unsettling for some of us. But stick with me and hear this out. The fear of the Lord is fear. Note how in verse 30 he says, We know him who said, Vengeance is mine, I will repay. We know him. Now, when all the people saw the thunder and the flashes of lightning and the sound of the trumpets and the mountain smoking, the people were afraid and trembled. Then Gideon perceived that he, the man he was talking to, was the angel of the Lord. And Gideon said, Alas, O Lord God, for now I have seen the angel of the Lord face to face. But the Lord said to him, Peace be to you, do not fear, you shall not die. Gideon wasn't in reverent awe, he was afraid he was a dead man. Uzzah put out his I'm quoting again. Uzzah put out his hand to take hold of the ark, for the oxen stumbled. And the anger of the Lord was kindled against Uzzah, and he struck him down, and David, that's King David. And David was afraid of God that day. And behold, the Lord passed by Elijah. And a great and strong wind tore the mountains and broke in pieces the rocks before the Lord, but the Lord was not in the wind. Little side note, therefore Elijah was unaffected, and he kept standing right where he was. Back to the quote. And after the wind an earthquake, but the Lord was not in the earthquake. And after the earthquake a fire, but the Lord was not in the fire. And after the fi And when Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his cloak and ran out of there. Finally. In the year that King Uzziah died, I saw the Lord sitting upon a throne high and lifted up. Woe to me, I cried, I am ruined. Not one of those examples approaches anything akin to reverent awe. These men and the one woman were scared. They were afraid. In the words of our author, they were fearful. Full stop. End of discussion. And it is precisely that same fear which our author invokes to keep his charges from making the fatal mistake of abandoning the Christian faith. Reverent awe should inspire our worship, but the fear of the Lord deters us from the ultimate and final foolishness of apostasy. So where does that leave us? Are we to cower before God, afraid of Him? Should we live in constant terror of the Lord of hosts? No and yes. Our author's argument does not lend itself to an easy answer, but it is an important one. He is seeking to drum up fear in the hearts and minds of believers. Hebrews, like all of the New Testament, was written for and to the church, for and to believers. Christians are the audience. And he wants those Christians, because the Spirit preserved it, we know the Christians here today as well, he wants them to be afraid. of God if they apostatize Do not imagine that God is some congenial old man, some friendly, grandfatherly type who will simply overlook any misstep and accept you any old way you come to him. Buddhism? Well, were you sincere in your Buddhism? Okay, great, come on into my heaven. Agnostic Dugeterism? Never quite sure if there was a God, but you hedged your bets by doing some good things. Fair enough. Come on into my heaven. That is not the true God. There is but one way to Him, and that is through Jesus Christ. You trample him underfoot, you profane his blood, you continue in sin by ignoring Christ's bride, and the full wrath of God awaits you. And that is the fear we are to have. That is the fear which keeps us out of trouble and is on that and keeps us on the straight and narrow. I can tell you that after that D in third grade spelling, for the rest of my pre-college career, my grades were A's and B's A little aside, not for nothing, something for parents and grandparents to ponder. If you want to raise children who have an experiential basis for understanding the fear of the Lord, Set expectations and enforce them. The mercy of God is not that he looks sin or lets disobedience slide. Do not think that slackness in parenting or grandparenting demonstrates mercy. It does not. The mercy of God is that he poured out his punishment on another and not on you He never relaxes his standard of holiness. Do not imagine that letting sin go unpunished in your home will somehow demonstrate God's grace. Let a little fear bring wisdom to your children. Anyway, back to our Hebrew text. Back to the question: Should I live in fear? Should you live in fear? But only in as much as they are tempted to walk away from the faith. In other words, there is to be fear and non-fear together at the same time in the believer. For those who believe, for those who live in Christ by faith, our author has already encouraged us to enter boldly the very presence of God, and to do so fearlessly. I'll tell you what, on my next report card I had an A in spelling. Did I bring that one home in fear? No, I burst into the house with joy and exuberance. I couldn't wait to show it off. I had nothing to fear because I was in right standing with the expectations. Just as those who are in Christ have been made perfect for all time. We have nothing to fear. And yet we must know that fear precisely, so that when our faith wanes and doubts overwhelm us, we don't cross into apostasy and abandon the faith. In the same way, we do not live in fear of God, yet that fear should be there to keep us safe, to keep us from falling into the hands of the living God. The fear of the Lord is not mere reverent awe, it is fear, it is dread, it is horror. Jesus Himself warned us that we should fear him who can cast both body and soul into hell. Yes, I tell you, fear him. That's not awe. That's terror We must be very afraid of God. It must be a part of our Christian life and our walk before the Almighty, but neither should we live in fear if we are in Christ. Without knowing the fear of the Lord and the hell he will bring to those who ignore him, or worse yet turn away from him, we are at risk of jumping off the edge of Christian doubt and into the peril below. But with that fear in our lives, we don't live paralyzed or overwhelmed. No, we appreciate the salvation Christ bestows We love the price he paid, and we live joyous, bold lives in God's presence. Do not live in fear But do not imagine navigating this life without a fear of the Lord. Because of the fear, you know you need the sacrifice of Christ. And because of the sacrifice of Christ, you know you needn't fear a sprite. Lord, this is a difficult subject. It is a hard thing for us to imagine both fear and non-fear residing in us simultaneously. And yet, Lord, we see that your inspired writer, the author of this book, pleads with Christians, warns them about the punishment that awaits those who turn away from the church and abandon Christ. And he wants them in fear to remain in faith. And in faith to boldly and fearlessly live in the presence of you. Lord, we ask for this tension in our own lives. That we would know the fear of the Lord, so that we would know Jesus Christ, so that we would know great joy. And when our faith is weak, when doubts overwhelm us, when we approach the edge and think about jumping out of the faith, remind us of what awaits such a person. Your anger, your wrath, your eternal hell. And let that keep us safe within Christ We pray this in His beautiful name. Amen.

But that's Paul's point. We don't look like that. That's not who we are in and of ourselves. In two weeks we're gonna do some cleaning around here, and the deacons wanna try to tackle the green shed. Now imagine for a moment that we get in there and we find this old broken pot. There are some old broken things out in that green shed. Despite this sermon, deacons, if you keep this, I will be most frustrated. But this is who we are. Broken. Worthless. Made of common materials. Made of the soil of the earth. Made of clay. We've busted ourselves up, we've soiled ourselves with dirt, we have got whatever fertilizer was used all over us And this is who we are. We're not those gold pitchers over there. We're broken pots. Deserving of the trash can. Deserving to be discarded by God. This is why the emphasis has been on mercy What is mercy? It's not getting what you deserve. It's not receiving the punishment that rightfully should be yours. And Paul says, if you're going to grasp salvation, if you're going to wrestle through the promises of Romans 8, then you've got to come to grips with Romans 9. This is humanity, every single one of us. God chooses in his divine compassion to take some broken pots and put them back together Mend them, glue them, fill in the holes, begin to rebuild them Imagine we find this and a few weeks later we we pull up one Sunday and there's this beautiful flowering plant out in front and it's got this gorgeous pot that's holding it and we're like, oh where'd that come from? And one of the deacons says Remember that broken pot we found in the shed? I put it back together and put it to that noble purpose. This is why there's no injustice in God. Would it be valid for the deacon to throw this away? Absolutely But God in his compassion chooses some of these broken pots to put back together. To patch, to paint, to beautify, to change from clay to gold, to make into something profoundly beautiful. For his purpose. So that. How many times have we heard the word purpose? All things work together for the good of those who've been called according to God's purpose. That his purpose and election might stand. God purposes broken people. And the only way that can be done would be through sovereign choice. There's no other way. The pock can't possibly make any claim. Look at me, I'm well suited to holding a beautiful plant. No All we can do is beg for mercy. And God chooses to be merciful. So how can we use that word hate? Because it is the only word that can fit out of the English language. When we regard what he does for the elect, when we understand that he chooses some and he rebuilds them and he remakes them and he reforms them and he puts them to noble use and he has a purpose for their life When that's the description of his love for them, those he passes by, he actively loves. God is love. He actively loves those whom he chooses. The ones, the the broken pots that he passes over, he doesn't actively smash them They weren't noble and perfect and in good shape, and he broke them. But the word hate is the fitting word For they get the opposite of what the elect get. They get the opposite of the love the elect receive. And so the only word that'll work is the opposite of love. But his love is active, his hate is not. His love is constructive, his hate is simply allowing. He does not destroy. And so this passage wrestles with this difficulty. Have we answered every question? No. We've still got more to read. We've got more to go in these three chapters. But Paul has said the first thing you gotta understand about salvation is that it belongs to our God. It is in his hands He will choose whom he saves. If you're wondering about the history of Israel, you first have got to deal with the fact that Israel was saved at all. And anybody from Israel would be saved. That God chose them at all is the miracle. That God had any compassion on anyone is the mystery. That some go to hell should not surprise that any go to heaven is a profound mystery. That this part would be thrown away is totally fitting. That it might be redeemed is by the amazing grace of God. Let's pray. Lord, these are difficult chapters filled with hard truths, and yet when we wrestle through them, when we see how you are at work in us. When we see that you are redeeming broken vessels, having mercy on those you choose to choose to have mercy, we are in awe of you. It is not as if it was just a question of you taking the time to piece together this fragmentary pot. No, to fix us cost you your son. What a profound thing that is. Let us never accuse you of being unfair, being injust. Let us never accuse you Of having a lack of compassion. For the very fact that you have called us to be your children is the proof that your compassion is profound. That your love is deeper and wider and richer than we could possibly comprehend You have taken us off from the floor of life's shed and redeemed us for your purposes. Let us rejoice in that truth. We pray this in Christ's name. Amen.

sermons.text: So it's the year thirty-three. It's late on the Monday night in Jerusalem. And though it's late, many people are laying awake. And it's not the weather, I know you're not that familiar with Jerusalem, but it's not the weather that's keeping them up. It's not that it's that particularly hot or cold. In fact, it's March 29th in the year 33 And temperatures in late March in Jerusalem are perfect for sleeping. Yet nobody can sleep. The city's quiet. But that's actually part of the problem. It's too quiet. It's eerily quiet. You see, this is festival week. This is Passover week. And in Jerusalem, during Passover week, the population of the city doubles. There should be people everywhere. There should be commotion. And yet there is not a cartwheel clattering or a foot falling on the streets outside. And it's because people are scared. On that Monday in Jerusalem, the things that have happened have frightened a great many people. And not knowing how it's going to play out, not knowing what's going to come of this They have hunkered down. They are in their homes. They are staying out of the way. The religious leadership, well, to say they're angry comes a little short of the mark. And they've promised action. And that's the problem. Nobody knows what action looks like. Nobody knows what this is going to be. And to complicate matters further, it's not just the Jewish religious leadership that people are uncertain about. This Galilean is stirring things up. This guy from up north seems to be at the heart of all the controversy, and it's not at all clear what he intends to do. Arguably, his parade into the city yesterday on the Sunday, arguably that was a provocative action. And then the madman scene in the temple this morning was undoubtedly provocative. It was over the top. It was downright weird. It's weird in any generic sense of the word, but it's particularly weird for this man called Jesus of Nazareth. Let me see if I can explain. Let me take you back a little ways in his ministry and remind you of where he's come from. Remember, we're talking about Jesus of Nazareth. He has been a carpenter-turned preacher. He's a no formal training, and yet he's got a following of students. He has did not grow up in Jerusalem. He did not grow up in the midst of all the religious activity of Jerusalem. And yet he has become a religious leader in his own right. He's from a little village called Nazareth, and if you can find that on a map, you're a better geographer than I am. And yet somehow he's got followers. And for the past three years, he's been preaching and teaching up in the north, up in Galilee. Which is not the place where people who want to be profound religious leaders tend to hang out. So why all the attention? Why has he garnered so much acclaim? Well, he's a miracle worker. Think about that. He's a miracle worker. Now a lot of us are skeptical. I get it. Somebody came up to us today and said they were a miracle worker, we'd be a little skeptical, and I think we'd be justified But this carpenter has garnered a following because of the signs and wonders he's performed. And they run the gambit. The first one recorded was the whole water-to-wine thing, right? But a lot of people can dismiss that, right? That's a conjurer's trick. That's a a magic act. That's a a parlor uh thing. It's flight of hand. But since then, he has caused the deaf to hear and the blind to hear. He's made the lame walk. He's cured leprosy. He's driven out demons. He has gone so far as to raise three people from the dead. Those are not parlor tricks. Those are not sleight-of-hand things. There's something going on with this guy, and he's become somewhat famous. But what's interesting about Jesus of Nazareth is that he's not famous primarily for his miracles. Arguably, his miracles take a backseat to his teaching and preaching. He teaches like no one else. He is described as having an authority not like any of the other rabbis Now we say authority, you know, there are some people who speak with authority on a subject because they are next level experts, if you will. I mean, who among us would argue with Brad Sears about wood turning? Or would debate with Chrissy about hairstyling? I certainly would not. They're experts in their fields. But to say that Jesus is an expert in that manner sells him short. For that's not really how he talks. That's the ordinary rabbis. They teach with that kind of acquired expertise. Jesus is teaching and preaching not as though he has come to understand the law, but as if he owns it. As if it's his to handle. When the when he preaches with authority, He says bold, brazen things like you've heard it said, but I tell you. He has up-ended our understanding of the law. And he's done so in such a profound and clear way that we kind of know that he's right. And yet he's done so in such a bold way that he has certainly angered a lot of people. He owns the law in an authoritative way. Now the picture I painted so far Sounds a little bit like maybe this guy's a glory hound, right? He does miracles, he teaches in brash, bold ways, he's all about the spotlight. And if that were true, then the parade yesterday and the temple tantrum this morning wouldn't be all that surprising. But you see, that's not who Jesus has been. Again, if you're not familiar, let me remind you. He's been quite the opposite of the Glory Hound. In fact, every time he's performed a miracle, he's commanded everyone to keep it to themselves, to tell no one. You remember the story of him healing the leper? And how is it recorded? He strictly warned him to tell no one. Strictly warned him. Not said, could you please keep it to yourself? Warned him. Don't tell anyone. Jesus heals the deaf man, and he tells him not to share with anybody. The way that got around, it makes you wonder if Jesus said it and then healed him. Because the guy seems not to have heard it. The dead girl. Her parents are going to be pretty stoked to get her back from the dead, right? And what does Jesus do in the room with the dead girl and Peter and James and John? He says, everybody keep their lips zipped. Don't talk about this. Don't tell anybody what has happened. Consistently Jesus has said, don't talk about me. Don't spread the word. Now you might be tempted to say, well, come on, Scott That's pretty clearly an advertising ploy. That is a really clever trick. That is reverse psychology, is what we'd call it today. By telling people not to talk about him, he's guaranteed that they're going to talk about him He's purposefully wording it that way, so that word about him will get out and he will appear humble. I don't think so. And here's why I don't think so. Consider the account of his teaching. Consider the account of the gathering. We remember that it wasn't all that long ago, a couple of years ago, that he had more than 5,000 men gathered to hear him preach. We know there were a bunch of women there, and there were probably some children in tow. We're looking at a crowd north of 12,000 people. Do you remember how it played out? If you're a glory hound, if you're all about the limelight, if you're all about yourself, what do you do with that crowd? Yeah, tell them what they want to hear. You give them what they want so they come back tomorrow, so that they bring their friends so the crowd keeps growing. But that's not what he does. He's got this huge crowd, and then he preaches the most bizarre doctrine. My body is real food. My blood is real drink. And if you don't eat of me and drink of me, you have no life in you. That's weird. That's not what you preach if you're trying to keep big crowds. And sure enough His good friend John records that by the end of that day, everybody had walked away mystified. Everybody had walked away disappointed, discouraged, thinking this guy has got to be losing his mind. He's insane. And in fact The crowd was so against him that day that John tells us that at the end of the day, Jesus wasn't even sure if the twelve would stay with him. Will you also leave me? He asked them. So it's not like he's preaching purposefully to get big crowds. In fact, just the opposite He has taken a megachurch and reduced it down to twelve people who aren't sure if they're staying. I don't think we can say that Jesus was applying some kind of reverse psychology when he said, don't talk about the miracles. And in fact, there seems to be a consistent message that he wants to fly under the radar, that he wants things to stay quiet. How many times do we read of him purposefully dodging the crowds? That he leaves them so he can go off and pray, that he gets in boats so he can get away from them. He's not seeking a huge follow. And that's what makes these past two days so strange. For three years he's been low profile. Keep it to yourself. Don't tell anybody. Oh, by the way, what has happened also during all that time? He's managed to anger the leadership. They are really ugly with him and have warned that they are going to try and capture him. So now think about it. It's festival week, it's Passover week. You're walking into Jerusalem. There are 30 or 40,000 other people walking into Jerusalem this week. It would have been a piece of cake for Jesus to pull his cowl up over his face and to just blend in with the crowd and slip in unnoticed. Celebrate the Passover with his little band of followers, slip back out and go back to Galilee. But you see that's not what he did. In fact what we have is this account of how he doesn't just walk into Jerusalem in the crowd, rather he rides into Jerusalem Now, I know you aren't first century Jews, so you may not appreciate that statement. But it was the custom of every Jew to walk into Jerusalem for the festivals. Even if you had the money to ride, if you could afford a cart or a horse or a donkey, you might ride from your hometown up to the outskirts of Jerusalem, but you dismounted. And you walked in. Why? Because that was a symbolic thing. It was to be to show that you're coming to the Passover because you need God's help. That you can't get through this life on your own. To ride in was to show off your wealth and your self-sufficiency. So even the very wealthy walked into Jerusalem. You say, well, that's just a symbolic thing. It is, but symbols are a big deal for Jews. And Jesus rode in. That is an astounding fact. So you're beginning to see why I said that Jesus' behavior was a little weird? Could have slipped in with the crowd, but he chooses to ride in. And as he rises in, what's going on? What's the scene that's happening? The crowds are singing the traditional psalms, Psalm 118 among them. But they're seeing them around him, purposefully. He's in the middle of all of the attention. One of the gospel writers tells us that the crowds ahead of him and the crowds behind him were singing antiphonally, that musical idea that you have one group that does one part and another group does another and they're physically separated from each other That's an antiphenal thing. And many of the psalms are set up to be antiphenal. We've read some of them that way. That I say one line, you say another That's how the Psalm 118 is set up. But the crowd isn't just randomly singing out the parts. No, there's a group in front of Jesus and a group behind Jesus, and Jesus is in the middle of it all. And what are they singing? Don't miss this. What are they singing? They're singing out Hosanna. Let me translate. It's quite simple. It means save us. Save us. They're singing out, Blessed is the king who comes in the name of the Lord, who comes in the name of Yahweh. You ever start to put those things together? They're saying, save us. They're saying, blessed is the king who comes in the name of Yahweh. Do you know what Jesus means? Do you know what that word, that name means? It literally means Yahweh saves. Now, if that's not a little heavy-handed, I don't know what is. In the middle of a bunch of people saying, Yahweh save us, the one named Yahweh Saves is riding on a donkey when everybody else is walking The whole thing almost appears choreographed and planned. Oh, by the way, what do they call out? Blessed is the king who comes in the name of the Lord? Little fact we may have missed. Two days earlier, on the Friday before Palm Sunday, Jesus and his followers are Walking from Galilee to Jerusalem. And along the way, there is a man, a blind man, Bartimaeus was his name. He calls out Son of David, have mercy on me. Now, there are a lot of people by this point along the road trying to get Jesus' attention. He chooses some interesting wording, son of David, and it gets Jesus' attention Jesus' disciples are first put off by this guy. Get out of the way of our teacher who's trying to get to Jerusalem, but Jesus pays attention to him. Now we can't miss the fact that he's called the son of David. David was the king, the king of the covenant, the king of the dynasty that God put in place. A son of David, a descendant of David, has a legal claim to the throne. So here he is being called as a son of David, and he's now riding into Jerusalem. And he's riding on a donkey. I know that doesn't translate into American culture particularly well, but the symbolism, we're back to that idea of symbols, the symbolism in the first century was not lost on those people. Generals ride into town on horses, beast of war. Generals ride into town with the threat of violence, and they're going to conquer you. Once the general has conquered, his king comes behind on a donkey. That was a symbol of peace. You are now under my thumb. You are now under my rule. We are no longer at war. I have conquered you. Therefore, we can be at peace. It is not lost on this crowd that this man is riding into Jerusalem on a donkey, to the sound of people saying, Blessed is the king who comes in the name of the Lord. And it is not lost on them that this is what the prophet Zechariah had foretold in Zechariah 9:9. O daughter of Jerusalem, behold, your king comes to you riding on a donkey. None of this is fitting. None of this befits the guy we've gotten used to saying, keep it quiet, don't talk about me, don't draw attention. This is profoundly provocative, and it absolutely draws attention. And at the end of it all, did you catch the what happens at the end of it all? One of the rig li religious leaders is walking apparently in the crowd and walks up to the donkey next to Jesus. And point out to Jesus how inappropriate this all is. This is not right, teacher. Tell your followers, tell your students to stop This is unbecoming. This is inappropriate. That you would be praised in this way, that you would be called a king in this way. And Jesus says, no, no, no. This has to happen. It must happen. If they stop proclaiming me as king, the rocks on the side of the road will do so. This is not happenstance. This is not coincidence. This is not that there's something going on here. And until I prepared to tell you this story, I'm not sure I realized it. But as weird as the parade was yesterday on that Sunday As out of character as that was, it's not the main reason for the unease, the disquiet in Jerusalem on Monday. That's got everything to do with what happened during the day on Monday. Sunday's parade was provocative, but it was nothing compared to the Manic Monday. You see, it's one thing to ride into Jerusalem like you own the place. To do so is to make yourself king. It is altogether something else to walk in the temple as if you own the place. To do so there is to make yourself God. The former will get you into a whole lot of trouble with the Romans, the latter will get you into a whole lot of trouble with God. And for sure it's going to infuriate the religious leadership. Oh, and by the way, whether you claim to be an earthly king or you claim to be God, both are capital offenses. In first century Jerusalem. You see it every turn, everything about Jesus over these past two days. Seems to point in the same direction. Now, there have been at least a half dozen previous times when people have wanted to arrest Jesus or kill Jesus. And he's always managed to slip away. Do you remember some of these? There was the time in Nazareth when Jesus was teaching in the synagogue. He compared himself to Elijah and he compared the people listening to him to the Israel in Elijah's day. That they were stubborn and hard-hearted. And the crowd in the synagogue gets angry and they drag Jesus, they haul Jesus out to a cliff at the edge of the village. And they are prepared to throw him over the cliff. And somehow he just slips away from their grasp. It was the earlier pilgrimage into Jerusalem when Jesus claimed to be sent by God. And they tried to arrest him on that occasion. And again, it doesn't we don't know for sure. It just kind of says he evaded them. And there was the shout showdown over ancestry. He claims the name of God and they are outraged and they pick up stones to stone him for blasphemy and he simply vanishes There are several other occasions we could talk about, but the point is the same. He seems always to escape this trouble It's as if he had like, you know, I don't know if he had Bilbo's magic ring or he, you know, he's got a cloak of invisibility. He can just poof be gone. But somehow he's always getting out of these binds. And so this morning, I digress a little bit there, this morning Jesus walks into the temple on Monday morning, and you know I don't know what else to say it. He kind of goes ape. You know that expression? Act like a gorilla? Start tossing things around your cage because you're angry? That's what he does. He's throwing things around the temple. But somewhere along the way, somebody had the right idea. You don't need to sacrifice a part of your flock Don't drag a lamb down from Galilee. Just bring some money and then you can buy one here in the temple and sacrifice it. That was never supposed to be the point. But now there are these animals, lambs for the people who had the money, doves, pigeons, the people who didn't have the money And Jesus is opening all their cages. It's a chaotic scene, folks. There are lambs bleaking and running everywhere. There are pigeons flying up in people's faces and hitting them and everything else There are adult men on the ground on their hands and knees trying to get the coins that have spilled everywhere before anybody else grabs their money. sermons.text: What does the condition of your life say about your relationship with God? What does the condition of your life say about your relationship with God? If you have a great job, a wonderful marriage, financial stability, does that mean that God loves you? When Jesus said, this is a fruit statement we know well, but when Jesus said It is easier for a camel to pass through the eye of a needle than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of heaven. When he said that, his disciples were aghast. The twelve, they stood slack-jawed in utter confusion. It was patently obvious to them that if you were rich, God loves you. On the other hand, if you lose your job, or if a loved one dies, a seemingly untimely death. Or if you suffer grave health concerns, is that evidence that you are on the outs with God? Perhaps he is angry with you. Perhaps he is punishing you. Maybe, maybe he's even abandoned you. Job's friends certainly thought that way, did they not? They blamed Job for all the bad things that had happened to him. And again, the twelve thought that way. When they encountered the man who had been born blind, they assumed God was punishing someone. Lord, they asked, who sinned this man or his parents that he was born blind? But God called Job righteous and said that there was nothing in him that had brought about all of his suffering. And Jesus said that the man born blind had nothing to do with either his sin or his parents. In the ancient world, it was very natural, very automatic to assume that your Situation in this life was a direct result of how the gods felt about you.
